articles.title: EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train
articles.summary: Russia's drone attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border has triggered EU calls to up support for Kyiv. Allies of Ukraine should show they "are not scared," said the bloc's top diplomat, Kaja…

image.caption: Top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas was among those to call for unity after Russia's attackImage: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several top EU politicians have called a Russian drone strike on a passenger train ​on Ukraine's border with Poland a bid by Moscow to intimidate Kyiv's allies that should be met with even more resolution.

In the incident, a drone hit the train's locomotive at a railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border, shortly after a diplomatic ‌train carrying former British ​Prime ⁠Minister Boris Johnson and other ⁠European ​diplomats had been at the station.

blocks.caption: Russia carried out two drone strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border on SundayImage: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did EU leaders say about the train attack?
"It [the attack] is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said.
"I ​think we should act the opposite. ​We should show that we are ⁠there ​for Ukraine ​and we are ​not scared," ‌she told reporters in ​Finland, ⁠where she attended ⁠a ​summit on Arctic strategy.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who was also at the meeting, said the attack demonstrated Russia's growing aggression and called both for more support for Kyiv and for harsher penalties on Moscow.

"For me, it means that we have to [...] do even more to help Ukraine, to support Ukraine. And we need more measures against Russia, more political measures, more sanctions, and make it clear that this is strong strategy," he said.
"We are united here in Europe," he added.
Amid Russia's war Ukraine, Poland reconcile painful past
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said the attack showed that Russia was "challenging all of us."

"We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it," he said.
French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack had a "very clear goal, which is to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, drive a wedge between them."
Barrot said Russian President Vladimir Putin had constantly stepped up pressure on the EU and NATO over the past five years.
"Why? Because he knows that our strength lies in our unity, and that as long as we stand together, nothing can intimidate us," he said.
Germany warns against escalation with Russia
German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius, for his part, called for caution.
"I take the drones that were approaching trains near the (Ukrainian-Polish) border very seriously, but we must not be forced into an escalation," he said.
The Kremlin has commented on the attack only by saying that the Russian army operated across all Ukrainian territory and would continue to do so.
Speaking about the incident on Sunday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has said Putin considered Russia to be "de facto" at war with Europe.
"Putin's terror is literally knocking at the door of the European Union and NATO," Sybiga said.

articles.title: ‘We are not scared,’ says top EU diplomat after Russian strike on passenger train
articles.summary: Kaja Kallas calls drone attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus ‘a message to the western world’
articles.byline: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and Charlotte Higgins and Amy Hawkins in Kyiv

blocks.text: Europe needs to show it will not be “scared off” in supporting Ukraine, the EU’s chief diplomat said, after a Russian drone hit a passenger train on the country’s border with Poland shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through.

The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus and running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said.
European leaders condemned the strikes on Monday. The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said the goal of the attacks was “to intimidate Europeans, discourage and above all divide them”.

The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Speaking on the sidelines of an Arctic conference in Finland, she said: “I think the question for us is what do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off, because otherwise, you know, Russia will just achieve what they want, which is the submission of Ukraine.”

A spokesperson for Kallas added: “We strongly condemn the latest Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border, including the attack against the passenger train,” and referenced a recent EU decision to approve a €6.1bn tranche of the €90bn loan for Ukraine. “We are acting on the front to equip Ukraine better to defend itself, and we will continue to stand firmly with Ukraine and its right to defend itself against Russian aggression,” the spokesperson said.

Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.
Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.

The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”

Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson, Petraeus and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.
The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone.
after newsletter promotion

The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.
“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.

He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.

articles.title: Zambians warned not to eat dead wildlife after anthrax kills dozens of animals
articles.summary: At least 12 people are being treated for anthrax after eating infected meat from wildlife carcasses.

blocks.text: Authorities in Zambia have warned people not to eat meat from wildlife after dozens of wild animals, including hippos, elephants, buffalo and a crocodile died following an anthrax outbreak.
A disaster management agency official said over the weekend that 12 people had been infected with the disease after consuming dead wildlife in the Munyamadzi River area.
The official urged the public not to consume meat from animals that die naturally or from unknown causes, while urging the public to report any such cases.
Authorities have also called for hunting in the affected area to be suspended until the extent of the disease and associated risks are established.
Officials have not yet ascertained the full geographical extent of the latest outbreak, with surveillance and laboratory investigations ongoing.

Anthrax is endemic to Zambia but human deaths are not common. In 2023, the country experienced what was described as an "unprecedented outbreak", which killed four people and spread to nine out of 10 provinces.
Another large-scale outbreak was reported in 2011, with more than 500 cases, when five people died after consuming meat from infected hippos.

In the latest outbreak in the Munyamadzi Game Management Area, in Muchinga province, Zambia's Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit said 46 hippos, eight elephants, five buffaloes and one crocodile had died since July.

"The sad story about the deaths of this wildlife is that the carcasses ended up being eaten by the local people - that's what they depend on for their food," said the unit's national coordinator Norman Chipakupaku.
No human deaths have been reported, and the 12 infected people are currently receiving treatment.
Anthrax is caused by a bacteria called Bacillus anthracis, which largely survives as spores that hide away in soil for years before entering an animal through inhalation or a cut or wound.
It mainly affects grazing animals and can lead to sudden death. It can be transmitted from animals to humans through contact with contaminated animal products.

Zambians have been urged not to consume, sell, distribute or handle meat from animals that have died suddenly or from suspected anthrax. The public has also been advised against handling wild animals.

articles.title: China criticises idea it is in 'malicious competition' over AI
articles.summary: It follows the Anthropic CEO 's calls for a slowdown in AI development, in a way that China doesn't pull ahead.

blocks.text: China has hit out against what it has called "threat narratives" over AI governance and warned against "engaging in confrontation and malicious competition".
It follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the AI race.
Over the past week, industry insiders at the leading US AI labs have been warning in extremely stark terms about the potential threat AI poses, with some saying it could wipe out humanity.
But US President Donald Trump has said his priority is making sure the US develops the tech faster than China.

China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday "narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest".
"All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good," he added.
His comments highlight the difficulties in getting agreement between the world's two leading AI powers.

An agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is "next to impossible", says Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor with the military studies programme at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
"As part of each state's core national security interests, cooperation in taking things slower and more safely in relation to AI, is very, very unlikely."

AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech. Despite US export bans on critical chips, Chinese AI innovation has been expanding, driven by open-source technology and Beijing's backing.
Many experts believe the US is still ahead, and Chinese firms are trying to catch up as they struggle to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars that investors are ploughing into American AI.

But Beijing, including Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself, has also spoken about the risks posed by AI. China must "balance development and security", and introduce and improve relevant laws and ethical guidelines, and strengthen prevention of risks, to "safeguard the interests of the people and national security", state security minister Chen Yixin wrote on Sunday.
He warned of the dangers of "hostile forces" such as foreign intelligence using AI and called for international cooperation.
"There are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks," Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote recently.
China has "technical reasons" to work with the US, she argues, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China, and detect and undertsand vulnerabilities.

In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, which aims to shape global AI governance. And speaking at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Xi proposed creating a community for open-source AI.

All this comes as calls for AI regulation grow louder in the US, especially after a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxson said last week that "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
Since then top industry bosses, such as Amodei, have called for a slowdown and more regulation.

"We need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities," Open AI's chief exective Sam Altman wrote on X on Monday, which was echoed by Microsoft boss Satya Nadella who said AI development "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities".
But US President Donald Trump downplayed the risks, saying that he wanted to keep the US's lead over China "because whoever wins AI, wins".

The competition is fierce. The former Anthropic employee Coxson told the BBC that there needed to be "some sort of coordinated slowdown with China, if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".
As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, South China Morning Post reports.

It is also likely to be part of the talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who are trying to meet before next week's summit, the paper said. Vice-Premier He runs the agency that oversees the country's economic planning, including AI development.
While collaboration between the US and China is important, experts say the nstakes are high for both countries.

"If China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, this will not be viewed in Washington as losing a technology race," says Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based firm, Forani Investments.
"It will be viewed as losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era."
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia

articles.title: Thousands demand end to violence in Mexican cartel hotspot
articles.summary: The city has seen violence skyrocket since a feud broke out between two rival factions of the Sinaloa cartel.

blocks.text: The march was scheduled to coincide with the second anniversary since the start of the conflict - which feud broke out after the arrest of wanted drug lord Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada in the US.
His followers, La Mayiza, allege he was betrayed by the son of the infamous founder of the Sinaloa cartel, Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán, and have turned on members of his faction, Los Chapitos.
The two factions regularly carry out ambushes, drive-by shootings and erect roadblocks by hijacking trucks, which they set alight.
Residents of Culiacán have been caught up in this internecine war.
Not only has the number of murders and disappearances shot up in the state but also those of extortions and robberies, official figures suggest.
Sunday's protest was organised by relatives of victims, local businesses, civil society groups and the Catholic church.
Businessman Sergio Esquer told AFP news agency that more than 5,000 businesses had closed since the start of the feud.
"That's the tragedy Sinaloa is experiencing," Esquer, who is a leader in the centre-left opposition party Movimiento Ciudadano, said.
The event started with a Mass in which the bishop of Culiacán called on members of the warring groups to put an end to their violence.

"Stop, look at what's happening, look at the affected families, look at the young people and at our city. No amount of power, of money, territory or ambition is worth more than a human life," he said.
Among those who attended the protest were relatives of a one-year-old boy who died after being hit by a bullet in the head during a shootout in the city last week.
As well as the wave of violence, Sinaloa state has also been hit by political upheaval in recent months.
In April, US prosecutors accused the state's governor, Rubén Rocha, and nine other current and former officials of conspiring with Los Chapitos to smuggle drugs into the US.
Rocha, who has denied any wrongdoing, stepped down temporarily while Mexican prosecutors opened an investigation of their own into the allegations.

Three weeks ago, he returned to his post, but just days later requested another leave of absence after President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on social media, without directly naming him that "power without principles becomes arrogance".

articles.title: Berlin businesswoman charged with spying for Russia
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the Berlin marketing executive used her political and military contacts to help a Russian intelligence officer gain access to influential circles and seek information on German…

image.caption: Prosecutors say the Russian intelligence officer whom Ilona W. allegedly assisted was based at the Russian Embassy in BerlinImage: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia.
Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power, according to the Federal Prosecutor's Office.
She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention.
What is Ilona W. accused of?
Prosecutors say Ilona W. ran a marketing agency in Berlin and also chaired a lobbying association, giving her extensive contacts in military and political circles.
She allegedly had contact with a full-time Russian intelligence officer at the Russian Embassy in Berlin from at least October 2023.
According to the indictment, she repeatedly supplied him with information about high-profile events and helped arrange access for him, in some cases under a false name.
Berlin detains German-Ukrainian woman for Russian espionage
Prosecutors say the aim was to allow the Russian intelligence officer to build up his own network for intelligence purposes.
What information was she allegedly seeking?
Ilona W. is also accused of attending events herself to identify useful contacts and potential targets.
Prosecutors say she tried to recruit people from Germany's Defense Ministry and the arms industry.
She also allegedly sought information on German defense policy and the defense industry on behalf of her Russian contact, particularly in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine.
The charges were filed last week before the state security division of Berlin's Higher Regional Court.
Germany expelled the suspected Russian intelligence officer linked to the case shortly after W.'s arrest, prompting Moscow to retaliate by expelling a German diplomat.
Edited by Natalie Muller

articles.title: What timing of a second referendum in Alberta could look like, if it were to happen
articles.summary: Albertans will vote next month on the possibility of a second referendum on separation, but exactly when that referendum — if a majority voted for it — would happen, remains somewhat murky.

image.caption: Albertans will vote on 10 questions in a referendum Oct. 19, including whether they support the province remaining in Confederation, or they support the province beginning the legal process to have a second, binding referendum on separation. (Janet French/CBC)

blocks.text: Albertans will vote next month on the possibility of a second referendum on separation, but exactly when that referendum — if a majority voted for it — would happen, remains somewhat murky.

The Oct. 19 referendum will include 10 questions, including whether Albertans would like to remain in Confederation, or if they support the province beginning the legal process of holding a binding referendum on separation.

Polls have consistently shown the majority of Albertans would prefer to stay in Canada, but polls aren’t outcomes. Political analysts expect turnout to be a key factor in determining whether a second referendum is necessary.
Elections Alberta said any questions about a future, second referendum must be directed to the provincial government.

items: What to expect when you’re voting in the Alberta referendum and watching results

blocks.text: “Should Albertans give us that direction in the Fall 2026 referendum, we would begin the legal process under the constitution to hold the binding referendum as soon as possible,” the premier’s press secretary Sam Blackett said in a statement.
Spring? Not spring?

In an audio recording from a UCP town hall in Lethbridge in August, Premier Danielle Smith is heard saying her goal would be to hold a binding referendum in spring 2027, if a majority of Albertans vote for it this fall.
Alberta content creator Lawrence Magee, who runs the account Berta Proud Dad, shared the recording.

In the audio, Smith says holding the vote in the spring would settle the issue before the next provincial election. That election is set for October 2027, though the premier can call a snap election before then.

Smith estimated in the recording a timeline of roughly two-and-a-half months of consultations, before the question would be finalized and submitted to the House of Commons for approval, and a vote scheduled for March or April.

“If this is truly going to [be] a referendum on those precise terms of departure, then there would likely have to be pretty long and pretty deep [consultations] and getting it done in a six-month stretch is extremely ambitious,” University of Alberta associate law professor Gerard Kennedy told CBC News.

But at a news conference on Aug. 26, Smith seemed to backpedal on that proposed timeline, citing the rules in the Citizen Initiative Act that prohibit a referendum from a citizen petition within a year of a general election.

Those remarks had some separatists fuming, including the Alberta Prosperity Project’s Jeff Rath, who rejected the idea the legislation is really any sort of an impediment to holding a binding referendum in 2027.
He suggested Smith is the real hurdle.
“As long as Premier Smith is premier of Alberta, Alberta will never be free,” he told hundreds of supporters outside the legislature late last month.

As to why the act prohibits citizen-initiated referendums in an election year, Kennedy says the reason is likely two-fold: both the burden on Elections Alberta, and the possibility that the issue could be one that comes up naturally in an election campaign.
But couldn’t that change?
“What [Smith] says isn't wrong, but it's not complete,” said Kennedy.
With its majority seat count, he says there is nothing stopping the government from simply changing the legislation.
“It would have to go through the legislative process, but they can do that quickly if they have to,” Kennedy said.

Plus, he says there’s nothing stopping the premier from calling a vote under the Referendum Act, which, unlike the Citizen Initiative Act, does not stipulate any kind of referendum black-out period before an election.
“Now, I don't think Elections Alberta would be very happy about that, because they are not exactly bored,” Kennedy said.
Under the Referendum Act, a separation vote could even be added as a ballot-box question during a provincial election.
But what makes sense politically for Smith is a separate question.

“If she were to call another referendum, let's say six months after the original referendum, six months ahead of a general election, there I think could be a very considerable political cost to pay,” said political scientist Lori Williams.
“Certainly she'd run into voter fatigue and a considerable backlash from those who object to being asked twice about a question that it's clear the majority of Albertans oppose.”
What needs to happen before a second referendum

In a news conference Sept. 1, Smith said she could not give a clear answer on when a theoretical second referendum might be held, because the court has “put a bit of a monkey wrench” in the situation.
Justice Shaina Leonard quashed a citizen-led petition on separation, ruling the government failed to carry out proper consultations with First Nations.
Smith says the government has not been given parameters as to what those consultations would need to look like.
The government is appealing the court’s decision, as is separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre, who led the petition drive.

It would be helpful, Kennedy said, to have those appeals dealt with first. The appeal court’s ruling — and potentially that of the Supreme Court, should the case go there — could help set the terms for what consultations look like.

Once the province has done consultations, it would need to settle on the wording of the referendum question. Within 30 days of that, the House of Commons would weigh in on the chosen question, as per the federal Clarity Act.

items: Can a province just decide to leave Canada? Here's what the law says

blocks.text: MPs would vote on the question, deciding if it is both clear and would result in clear expression of the will of the province.
Because the Clarity Act was enacted in 2000, following the last Quebec sovereignty referendum, it would be the first time it would be tested.

“We are in uncharted territory. Like, if the province said ‘we don't care what the Clarity Act has to say,' that might be pragmatically unwise, but it's not necessarily doomed to legal failure,” Kennedy said.
However, given the polls that show majority support lies on the remain side, Kennedy doubts that it will be put to the test in this case.
“Do you want what my best prediction is? There's nowhere near a majority vote yes in the Oct. 19 referendum and this is all a moot point.”

items: 18m agoTrump's mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge

blocks.text: Trump's mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
A second ⁠federal ⁠judge has prevented ⁠Donald Trump’s administration from implementing ⁠a ​new ‌US ‌Postal Service ‌rule that would tighten mail-in voting requirements.

However, ‌the US Supreme Court is ​still weighing the administration’s ⁠request to ​overturn a separate ​order ​blocking the ​rule. Late on Sunday, District Judge Carl J Nichols in Washington, DC, handed down a similar hold on the rule, which was issued 21 August.

“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that, absent an injunction, there is an increased risk that a significant number of otherwise appropriate absentee or mail-in ballots will ultimately not be counted in the upcoming elections,” Nichols wrote in issuing the preliminary injunction.
“The public has a strong interest in ensuring that doesn’t happen.”

Nichols in May had refused to issue an injunction because he ruled the lawsuit seeking one was brought too early. That was the high court’s reasoning late last month when it lifted an earlier freeze by Talwani.

But because the administration had just issued its rule to move ahead with Trump’s plan, the plaintiffs in Boston and Washington, DC, refiled their lawsuits. Talwani was nominated by former president Barack Obama and Nichols was nominated by Trump.

The new Postal Service regulations stem from an executive order Trump issued earlier this year. Election officials say it would be impossible to implement the changes this close to a general election.

articles.title: Pay to ghost your boss: Japan's resignation business
articles.summary: Resignation agencies in Japan help employees seamlessly erase themselves from a job in just 15 minutes, and young people are especially eager to use their services.

image.caption: Like ghosting in dating, Japan's bakkure refers to suddenly vanishing from a job Image: Morio Taga/Jiji Press Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Y.M., a Japanese man in his early twenties, his first job out of university at a real estate sales firm quickly turned into a daily trial of endurance. Among his colleagues, he was always the one being screamed at.

According to his testimony featured on the website of Leadbrain, a Tokyo-based labor and human resources consulting firm, he sought a quiet way out because he was wary of how colleagues perceived him. He was reluctant to burden his parents, and determined to avoid workplace conflict, which is a common attitude among working Japanese. Rather than submitting a resignation in person, he opened his phone and began searching for a resignation proxy service — a third-party agency to help him quit his job without direct interaction with his employer.

In Japan, vanishing from a workplace without notice is known as bakkure, a concept somewhat parallel to "ghosting" in modern dating. For many foreigners, leaving a job without notice would be considered an irresponsible and hurtful act. But within the logic of Japanese social interactions, vanishing is a way to avoid direct conflict and maintain harmony — at least on the outside.
Pay to flee

The commercial demand for these resignation agencies is booming. Albatross, one of Japan's leading businesses of this kind, helps about 450 people quit without confrontation every month. They charge roughly €120 ($138.5) per client working a full-time job. The majority of these clients are young professionals in the service industry and manufacturing. The process can be completed within 15 minutes.

blocks.caption: In a conflict-avoidant society, using resignation proxy services to quit your job is a common practice Image: Takaya Suzuki/Jiji Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The reasons why people requested us to resign for them range from physical violence to sexual harassment," said Yuka Hamada, the CEO of Albatross. "They are vulnerable in this case, and they are not brave enough to quit their job."
Around 1 in 3 people reported experiencing some form of harassment at work, according to a survey of Japanese workers aged 20 to 49 by consulting firm Shikigaku.
Harmony above all else

Traditional Japanese corporate culture originated during the post-World War II economic boom and relies heavily on the "lifetime employment" system. In this culture, loyalty is regarded as the highest virtue, and bosses often view resignations as insults, so many young employees fear resigning in person.

"Announcing one's intention to resign can feel not merely like ending a contract, but like disappointing others or betraying expectations that one has previously continued to meet," said Hiroki Nakamori, an associate professor at Rikkyo University's Graduate School of Social Design Studies.

Japan is a non-confrontational culture, and people are expected to fall in line when making certain commitments to the company and the company's culture. "Those who disturb the harmony are not appreciated, so someone leaving might feel they should just disappear without making too much of a fuss," said Hiroshi Ono, a professor of Human Resources Management at Hitotsubashi University Business School.
"Acting in a collective and acting in harmony is a sign of strength," added Ono.

This cultural compulsion to avoid conflict runs deep. Even Japan's Seventeen-Article Constitution — the 7th century foundation of modern Japanese governance — explicitly states: "Harmony should be valued and quarrels should be avoided."
Ghosting with consideration

But ghosting a job can also be done in a polite way. "Clients may not say goodbye or express their gratitude directly to the company. In such cases, the agency can deliver these words on their behalf," says Albatross CEO Hamada.

It is the ultimate paradox of Japanese workplace culture: Even in the act of ghosting, the employee feels compelled to abide by meiwaku — the social obligation of minimizing trouble for others and preserving collective order above all else. This also applies to removing their personal items from the workplace.
"Even if a client intends to completely vanish from their job, we still advise them to clear off their desk" before leaving, added Hamada.

articles.title: Senate okays 5-year term for barangay, SK officials
articles.summary: The Senate on Monday approved on third and final reading a bill seeking to extend the term of office of barangay officials and members of the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) to five years.

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 6:23pm
The Senate on Monday approved on third and final reading a bill seeking to "fix" the term of office of barangay officials and members of the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) to five years.
With 13 affirmative votes, five negative votes, and no abstentions, the upper chamber approved Senate Bill No. 2387 during its plenary session.
Voting against the measure were Senators Vicente Sotto III, Bam Aquino, Joel Villanueva, Francis Pangilinan, and Risa Hontiveros.
Sotto said he will file a "turno en contra" (vote against) explaining his opposition to the approval of the measure.
The measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 12232 by extending the current four-year term of barangay and SK officials to five years.

It also provides that no elective barangay official shall serve for more than two consecutive terms in the same position, while no elective SK official shall serve for more than one term in the same position.

The bill also proposes moving the next regular Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) from the first to the second Monday of November 2028, with succeeding elections to be held every five years thereafter.

Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, the measure’s principal author and sponsor, said the five-year term would give barangay and SK officials more time to plan, implement, and evaluate programs before the next elections.
“Barangays are planners, implementers, first responders, peacekeepers, and frontline service providers — all at a level where government interacts directly with households and families,” he said.
“With a five-year term, our officials will have more time to implement programs and projects that will truly benefit their communities,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Israeli minister accuses 'NAZA' filmmakers of 'treason'
articles.summary: Israel's culture minister wants to strip the makers of a documentary on Israel's Gaza offensive of their citizenship. He accused the two of seeking "applause from antisemites around the world."

image.caption: Filmmakers Rachel Szor (L) and Yuval Abraham received the Special Jury Award in Venice on SaturdayImage: Wang Kaiyan/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has threatened to strip filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of their citizenship after the two won a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival for a documentary about Israeli airstrikes killing Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

The film, called "NAZA" — a Hebrew acronym said to be used for counting the estimated number of civilians to be killed in a military strike — contains interviews with Israeli intelligence operatives behind the attacks.
Israel's military denies deliberately targeting civilians.
What did the culture minister and others say?
Zohar said Abraham and Szor were "willing to harm their homeland in order just to get applause from antisemites around the world."
"I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state," Zohar wrote on X.
Far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir also used the platform for a post in which he called the two filmmakers "a disgrace and an embarrassment" to Israel.

The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, with the Supreme Court confirming in 2022 that the state may strip people of their nationality for acts of "disloyalty" such as espionage or treason.
What does the film 'NAZA' show?
For "NAZA," Abraham and Szor spoke to 24 Israeli military or intelligence personnel in nighttime interviews on rooftops in Tel Aviv.

Those interviewed gave details on the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza in Israel's offensive in retaliation for the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which killed around 1,200 people in Israel.

blocks.caption: Interviews for the documentary were held in Tel AvivImage: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to figures by Gaza officials, which are considered to be broadly reliable by the UN, more than 73,000 Palestinian people, including 20,000 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks since the operation began.

Abraham said "the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanization of Palestinians."

The Israeli army has rejected allegations made in the 80-minute film, among other things criticizing the use of anonymous testimonies and saying the identities of the whistleblowers could not be verified.

articles.title: $5.5M daycare built with provincial funds now derelict, scavenged by thieves and damaged by flooding
articles.summary: A $5.5-million Winnipeg-area daycare built two years ago with provincial funds sits vacant, derelict and surrounded by weeds after being plundered by scavengers and damaged by flooding.

image.caption: Weeds grow around a $5.5-million daycare built in East St. Paul with provincial funds in 2024. It's been vacant since, even though the daycare operator waiting to use the building has 800 kids on its waiting list. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

blocks.text: A $5.5-million Winnipeg-area daycare built two years ago with provincial funds sits vacant, derelict and surrounded by weeds after being plundered by scavengers and damaged by flooding.

The non-profit group hoping to operate the daycare and an advocate for not-for-profit daycares are now pleading with the province to open the East St. Paul facility, which has yet to care for a single child.

The 74-space daycare was built in 2024 on behalf of the Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust. It was one of 22 daycares built in Manitoba as part of a project started by the former Progressive Conservative government along with JohnQ Public, a company owned by 11 Manitoba municipalities.
The structure has been vacant since, even though the daycare operator waiting to use the building has 800 kids on its waiting list.
The provincial government has said this is because a change of land ownership has contravened the daycare's operating agreement.
CBC News took a tour of the daycare last week and documented extensive damage to both the interior and exterior of the building.
Vacant daycare built 2 years ago derelict, ransacked by thieves
"It's heartbreaking and frustrating," said Patrick Ryan, the volunteer board chair for Created 4 Me Early Learning Centre, which has been stymied in its efforts to move into the building.
The tour of the daycare revealed broken windows inside the facility, broken glass on the floor and damage to the building's security system.
Two commercial fridges and a dishwasher are missing and presumed stolen. Copper wire has been stripped from inside and outside the building.

Air-conditioning units on the daycare's roof have been partly dismantled, with mechanical parts missing — presumably removed by scavengers — and rainwater has penetrated the building, damaging ceilings. The building went months without power, meaning its sump pump didn't run and about half a metre of water has pooled in the basement.
Selkirk RCMP investigated the damage but said they did not identify any suspects.
Ryan estimated the damage to the as-yet-unused daycare exceeds $1 million.
"It's frustrating from the perspective of the amount of money that the public has put into the facility to see the building in the state that it is," he said.
His organization hired staff to work at the daycare but had to let them go after making repeated attempts to get the centre open.
The executive director of Created 4 Me says the situation has been "very difficult."
"It is very difficult to plan for the unknown, without an opening date being set, or being pushed back," said Laura Van Landeghem.
"It has been emotionally draining."
Provincial funds stopped flowing in 2024

The daycare was built for Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust, an arm's-length entity formed by Manitoba's most populous First Nation to acquire real estate for investment and housing for the benefit of band members, according to its founding documents.

The daycare is built on part of a former golf course east of Highway 59 called The Meadows, purchased by the trust in 2021. The placement of the daycare on land located more than 150 kilometres south of the First Nation's main reserve led some band members to criticize the decision to build in East St. Paul.

In 2024, the Peguis real estate trust sold 75 per cent of a company that controls the Meadows land to a numbered company owned by Andrew Marquess, a former adviser to the trust, according to a purchase and development agreement obtained by CBC News.
Manitoba paid out $3.3 million of the $5.5 million budgeted for the daycare before funding for the project stopped flowing in November 2024, according to the province.

According to a letter tabled in the Manitoba Legislature the following April, former deputy minister of education and early childhood learning Brian O'Leary said the project may not have followed normal provincial or municipal procurement practices.
In January, Manitoba Education and Early Childhood Learning Minister Tracy Schmidt said the province had an agreement with Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust.
"Our understanding is right now they do not own that land," Schmidt said at the time.

items: $5.5M daycare built with provincial funds still not open because government can't figure out who owns the land

blocks.text: "We need to ensure the long-term viability of this project, so we need to ascertain that the agreement is in compliance. Once we have certainty about the long-term viability of this product, we'll proceed as soon as possible."
Eight months later, Schmidt said the province still has not received documentation from Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust to demonstrate who owns that land.
"Until we receive documentation assuring government who owns the land, we can't proceed," she said earlier this month in an interview in her office.
"Me and my team have been in constant communication with legal counsel, and we are pulling every lever available to us to make sure we can get the centre open as soon as possible."
A lawyer for Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust did not return requests for comment.
Schmidt said she could not provide a timeline for getting the daycare open because the province is not the legal owner of the property.
"If I could walk down there tomorrow … and open it up myself, I would do that, and I think the premier would come with me. We are doing everything that we can."
Delay puzzling: advocate

The delay in getting the East St. Paul daycare open is baffling, said Gerrie Prymak, a retired teacher who now advocates for child care and helped found Little Stars Playhouse daycare in Winnipeg's North End.
Prymak said Little Stars had to enter into an operating agreement with the province before it could open, and questioned why the provincial government can't cut through the bureaucracy in this case.
"I don't know why it's taking a year and a half," Prymak said in an interview at Little Stars on Selkirk Avenue.
She urged Premier Wab Kinew to get personally involved.
"[Have] a face-to-face meeting and say, 'Children first.… We've got to get this open,'" she said.
Kinew said Thursday he is "always down to meet."
Prymak said she went to visit the daycare site herself when she heard it still wasn't open.
"When I saw the vandalism, I thought, 'what a waste,'" she said. "Why can't there be some security that they can pay for to take care of this piece of property that we invested so much money for?"
Prymak also said the province has fallen short of its 2021 promise to create 23,000 daycare spaces by March of this year.
The NDP government said in August it has created or promised to open 12,700 spaces since taking power in 2023.
Schmidt said the province is still working to create more daycare spaces.

"While I understand that every single space counts, and that families are relying on these 74 spaces in East St. Paul to open as soon as possible, Manitobans should rest assured that our government is working as hard as we can to meet that need," she said.
In the meantime, Patrick Ryan is encouraging more action from the province to get Created 4 Me daycare open.

"We're really calling on the provincial government and the Rural Municipality of East St. Paul to step up and do what it takes to get this place open," he said, adding he has had reasonable conversations with all parties involved.
"Everybody has an interest in getting this place opened. Call on everybody to sit down together and figure out a plan to get it open."

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian gets marriage ribbing from fellow senators over SALN query
articles.summary: Senators Francis Escudero and Francis Pangilinan teased Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian about possibly getting married after a witness in Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial explained…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 14, 2026 5:52pm

Senators Francis Escudero and Francis Pangilinan teased Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian about possibly getting married after a witness in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial explained why public officials must include their spouses’ assets in their Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

Gatchalian, a bachelor, drew the ribbing after he asked a prosecution witness, former Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang, why a public official’s SALN should include the assets of the official’s spouse when the couple jointly files the document.
One of the allegations in the impeachment complaint against Duterte is that she accumulated unexplained wealth by:

items: failing to fully and truthfully disclose all her and her spouse’s assets, liabilities and net worth in her SALNs, including those for 2022, 2023 and 2024; and
failing to divest herself of, and instead continuing to wilfully maintain, all her business interests while serving as vice president in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

blocks.text: Cabotaje-Tang explained that under the Supreme Court’s ruling in Babano v. Executive Secretary, a public official must declare the assets of his or her spouse in the SALN unless the couple entered into an agreement for a complete separation of property before their marriage.

“If the married couple came up with a [pre-nuptial] agreement of a complete separation of property, then the government official does not need to declare the assets of his or her spouse in his SALN. Without such agreement, all assets of the spouse must be declared in the SALN of the public official,” Cabotaje-Tang said during her testimony on the 24th day of Duterte’s impeachment trial.
Gatchalian also asked Cabotaje-Tang whether these assets included cash.
“Yes, Sir,” the witness replied.

Cabotaje-Tang said the law penalises a public official’s intentional non-declaration of a spouse’s assets, including removal from office under Section 8 of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act in cases involving the unlawful acquisition of unexplained wealth.

She also cited the Supreme Court’s ruling in Rabusa v. Republic, saying the wife of retired Army lieutenant colonel George Rabusa should be able to establish that she legitimately acquired properties attributed to her.
“In the case of Rabusa v. Republic [Supreme Court decision], his wife should be able to show she legitimately acquired those properties," Cabotaje-Tang said.

Otherwise, if she fails to show that she has the financial capacity to acquire those assets and these assets are traceable to the public officials, that becomes the property of the public official, including businesses, provided that the ownership of those [business] assets are traceable to the public official,” she added.
This prompted Escudero to interject.

“Salamat po sa payo niyo, Justice [Cabotaje-Tang], kung sakaling dumating man also chimed in.po ‘yung panahong ‘yun kay SP (Senate President), alam na po niya kung paano niya idedeklara sa kanyang SALN ‘yung asset ng kanyang mapapangasawa,” Escudero said on Monday.
(Thank you for your piece of advice, Justice Cabotaje-Tang. When the time comes for SP to get married, he would already know how to declare his spouse’s assets in his SALN.)
Senator-judge Pangilinan also chimed in: “Baka merong alam si Senate President na hindi natin alam tungkol sa mga plano niyang pag-aasawa base sa mga katanungan,”
(Maybe the Senate President knows something that we don’t about his marriage plans, based on his questions.)
Both Escudero and Pangilinan are married to movie actresses who had acquired substantial assets before their respective marriages.
Escudero married actress Heart Evangelista in 2015, while Pangilinan married actress and singer Sharon Cuneta in 1996.

Ahead of Gatchalian’s questioning, Cabotaje-Tang testified during direct examination that government investigators may scrutinise the assets of public officials’ spouses and children “to prevent a circumstance that a public official is able to evade investigation.”— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Cayetano siblings float alleged threats vs some senator-judges
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and Senator Pia Cayetano on Monday raised concerns about supposed threats and intimidations against them.

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 5:41pm
Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and Senator Pia Cayetano on Monday raised concerns about supposed threats and intimidations against them.

On the 24th day of the impeachment trial, Pia Cayetano asked Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang if she encountered situations where judges, because of their professions, received threats in public.
Tang said there were none, in relation to pending cases before the Sandiganbayan.
“I’m happy for you kasi kami ho meron (because we have),” Pia said.
Alan Peter, in jest, also asked Tang during the trial if she can issue a writ of amparo to senator-judges who are being intimidated, since her first name is Amparo.

The writ of amparo is available to persons whose rights to life, liberty, and security are being threatened or violated by public officials, employees, or private individuals or entities. It covers extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, or threats.
In an ambush interview, Alan Peter said the threats were allegedly being made to opposition senators.

“Obvious naman, ‘di ba guys? I mean, obvious naman. You can see it with your eyes. When Senator Ping, as an example, says, dapat matapos ‘yung impeachment by December, then by December may kaso daw ako. The changing of the numbers. Sino ba kinakasuhan? ‘Yung nasa oposisyon,” the minority leader said.

(It’s obvious, isn’t it, guys? I mean, it’s obvious. You can see it with your own eyes. When Senator Ping, for example, said the impeachment should be finished by December. They’re saying that by December, I’ll be facing charges. Then there’s the changing of the numbers. Who are being charged now? Those in the opposition.)
Asked who is behind the threats, he said, “Alangan naman ang opposition mag-threaten sa kapwa opposition?”
(It wouldn't make sense if those in the opposition are the ones threatening fellow members of the opposition, would it?)
“Let's open our eyes. If we want to see the truth, all we have to do is open our eyes,” he added.
GMA News Online reached out to the office of Lacson for a comment and will update this story once it responds. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Swedish centre-left opposition widens lead to three seats with 95% of votes counted – Europe live
articles.summary:
The parliament isn’t set to meet until late September to elect a new speaker, and then prime minister

Senior figures in the Social Democratic party are meeting this morning with…

blocks.text: Morning opening: When the dust settles (a bit)

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Hej from Stockholm as the dust settles (a bit) after a hectic election night.

With 95% of votes counted overnight, the left-leaning opposition bloc – led by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – has widened its lead to three seats, leading 176 to 173 against the reigning centre-right coalition and their far-right partners in Sweden Democrats.

blocks.caption: Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson gives a speech during the party´s election watch after the Swedish parliamentary election in Stockholm. Photograph: Caisa Rasmussen/BILDBYRÅN/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Formally, the result is not settled yet: there is only some 28,600 votes separating the two blocs, with 6% of the votes yet to be counted – and that includes some 200,000 votes expected to come and be counted only on Wednesday.
Still, the Swedish public broadcaster SVT said last night it was 90% confident that the opposition would clinch the victory, even accounting for all the votes yet to be counted.

There is plenty of time for early exploratory talks: the parliament won’t meet until 28 September, when its due to elect a new speaker, and any votes on who could be the next prime minister can only come after that.
But the process of forming the new government could take weeks if not months leaving Sweden in a state of political limbo at a time of unprecedented geopolitical uncertainty in Europe.
No doubt first text messages, frantic WhatsApp or Signals, and phone calls are already exchanged today.
I will be here to cover all this drama for you.
It’s Monday, 14 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 2m agoPM Kristersson wants to 'take it easy' and wait until final results
26m agoSocial Democrat leadership meets for talks after election win
36m agoMorning opening: When the dust settles (a bit)

blocks.text: PM Kristersson wants to 'take it easy' and wait until final results
Perhaps we should all just channel the Swedish PM, Ulf Kristersson, who essentially said this morning he was “going to take it pretty easy” until the final results are in.

blocks.caption: Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson of the Moderate Party leaves the official residence, Sager House, a day after the Swedish general election in Stockholm, Sweden. Photograph: Claudio Bresciani/EPA

blocks.text: He says there are some conversations scheduled in the meantime – including with fellow coalition leaders this evening – but he essentially wants to see the final results show first.
He also repeats his last night’s suggestion of exploring alternative majorities in the parliament.
One possible option could involve the Centre party switching sides, but it’s not immediately obvious how Kristersson would get them to accept a government with the far-right Sweden Democrats with it.
Social Democrat leadership meets for talks after election win
Senior figures in the Social Democratic party are meeting this morning with party leader Magdalena Andersson to discuss next steps.

blocks.caption: Social Democrats party leader Magdalena Andersson (L) arrives at the Social Democrats election night watch party in Stockholm, Sweden. Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The party topped the polls – that is certain – and is most likely to have a first go at forming the next government, but it will have to navigate the complex and often openly contradictory demands of the left-leaning bloc.
It remains to be seen whether they can get the Left Party to work with the Centre Party in particular, given rumbles on both sides about the feasibility of such an alliance.
But today’s doorstep comments suggest there is no rush just yet: all parties will want to wait for the final results on Wednesday or Thursday before committing to exploratory talks.
Party secretary Tobias Baudin confirmed, however, that he has exchanged texts with colleagues in other parties, SVT reported.
Asked about potential differences, he told P1 that he was “completely convinced” the parties would give it out with some “give and take” for all involved.

articles.title: Sara Duterte defense brings up Marcos business interests in SALN at impeachment trial
articles.summary: The defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday raised before the impeachment court President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.'s financial interests in some companies, as reflected in a…

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 5:32pm

The defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday raised before the impeachment court President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.'s financial interests in some companies, as reflected in a Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), which the prosecution had objected to.

This developed in the cross-examination of former Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang. Presented as an expert witness by the prosecution, Cabotaje-Tang earlier testified that the President and Vice President were barred from participating in any business because of the greater possibility of abuse of power in their respective offices as the country’s two highest government officials.

Prosecutor Akbayan party-list Rep. Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno objected to the presentation of the SALN, saying the prosecution had no way of knowing “if what counsel is showing is an authenticated copy of the SALN. We have no way of knowing if that actually belongs to or was filed by the President.”
Presiding officer Senator-Judge Francis “Chiz” Escudero allowed the question, saying the document could be properly marked at a later time.

“A while ago, you mentioned that a President or a Vice President is absolutely prohibited from having financial interest in companies. Tama po ba? Dito po kasi sa SALN ni Presidente as of December 31, 2025, meron pong mga nakalistang…mga business and financial interests sa mga kumpanya,” Vinluan asked Tang.

(A while ago, you mentioned that a President or a Vice President is absolutely prohibited from having financial interests in companies. Is that right? Because here in the President's SALN as of December 31, 2025, there are listed... business and financial interests in companies.)
“So are you saying that this falls under what you mentioned about absolute prohibition in business and financial interest?” he added.
Before Tang, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel, answered, Diokno cut off, reiterating his objections.
“We have no way of knowing if what counsel is showing is an authenticated copy of the SALN; we have no way of knowing if that actually belongs to or was filed by the President,” Diokno said.
Escudero said he believed the defense will be making the necessary marking “at the proper time.”
Vinluan also stressed that the document is “publicly available” and was reported by a particular news outlet.
“Just the fact that it’s publicly available and reported by the news does not authenticate it, Your Honor,” Diokno said.
Vinluan countered, saying the presiding officer has already ruled on the matter.
“I’m just responding, Your Honor, to the statement of the defense counsel. Ayoko pong makipag-away [I don’t want to fight],” Diokno said.
Vinluan said, “Ako rin po [Me too].”
Escudero said, “Not your character, Honorable Chel.”
Tang opted not to answer the question from the defense. Vinluan, in response, said he respects the refusal of the former Sandiganbayan justice.

Earlier during the trial, Tang explained that the President and Vice President are barred from participating in any business because of the greater possibility of abuse of power in their respective offices, being the country’s two highest government officials. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Finland: EU leaders meet to forge new Arctic policy
articles.summary: European leaders are meeting over shipping, resources and security in the region amid pressure from the US, China and Russia. The EU sees the Arctic as key to its future security as melting ice makes…

image.caption: European leaders are in Finland to plot the increasingly important Arctic region's futureImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: European leaders are gathering in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Monday to plan a path forward for the bloc's presence in the Arctic.
The talks will focus on emerging shipping lanes, raw mineral deposits and security threats from the US, China and Russia.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, the prime ministers of Estonia and Latvia, the presidents of Lithuania and Romania, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and EU Council President Antonio Costa are all scheduled to attend Monday's "European Arctic Summit."

"The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably," according to Tuomas Tikkanen — Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's senior adviser on European affairs.
Orpo, who initiated the summit, has emphasized that the Arctic is an, "increasingly important part of Europe's security environment."

Finland also insists European icebreaker capabilities are included in the strategy, saying they are key to Europe's ability to operate in the High North, adding that without them it would be impossible to protect supply and trade routes, or military presence across the region.
NATO drills highlight Iceland's role in Arctic defense
EU will use meeting to shape its new Arctic strategy
No formal decisions are expected Monday, but the European Commission has said the talks will help shape its new Arctic strategy, which will be unveiled over the next few weeks.
National leaders can still have a say impacting the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," said Finnish adviser Tikkanen.
The bloc's last strategy paper was released in 2021.
The Arctic, which is warming nearly four times faster than other regions, has seen increased activity as receding ice opens potential transport routes as well as access to mineral resources.
That changing environment has spurred the US, China and Russia to increase energy, resource and military activity.
In August, China and South Korea both sent container ships through the region, testing the viability of the North Sea Route in Russian territorial waters.
Russia's Arctic buildup is Iceland's security headache
As Arctic ice melts, desire for control of the Arctic has heated up

Although Canada, China, Russia and Scandinavian countries are all considered Arctic nations, the most concerning development of late for the EU and member state Denmark have come from an entirely unexpected corner — the United States.

US President Donald Trump has threatened to blow up the NATO military alliance through his insistence that "the US must have Greenland" — a semi-autonomous island nation that is officially Danish territory — citing national security concerns, even threatening to take it by force if necessary.
Trump argues that Denmark cannot protect Greenland, which is not part of the EU, from China and Russia.
NATO has since launched a new security mission in the region.

Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, on a visit to Greenland, also announced closer cooperation and an investment package of €200 million ($231 million) to be used in part to set up infrastructure to extract valuable raw materials.

During her visit, von der Leyen vowed that the EU would "be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic," saying the package would "create new opportunities and a strong and engaged EU in both Greenland and the Arctic."
Why the US and Europe are battling for Greenland's future

articles.title: Richard Tice accuses Labour of ‘trying to change rules retrospectively’ after Reform receive £72m in donations – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Labour MPs and unions are pressuring the government to legislate for a stricter cap on political party donations

Richard Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, has declined to say…

blocks.text: Reform declines to say if £72m donors returned to UK within 12-month limit
Richard Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, has declined to say when two crypto billionaires who gave a combined £72m to the party returned to the UK, Peter Walker reports.
Richard Tice accuses Labour of using retrospective law 'dictatorship' tactics to block Reform UK donations

Good morning. This afternoon peers will debate the second reading of the representation of the people bill. If you hear a loud bang echo around the Lords chamber, it will be the sound of the stable door being shut after the horse has bolted.

At the end of 2024 the Sunday Times carried a report saying that Elon Musk was considering donating $100m to Reform UK. It made a good headline, but the idea seemed so preposterous that no one at Westminster really took it very seriously. Musk is not a British citizen, and so it would have been illegal for him to have given the money directly anyway; he would have had to have donated via UK companies.

Musk is now backing Restore Britain. But of course there are British billionaires who support Reform UK too. Some Labour MPs (including Andy Burnham himself, at one point) have always been in favour of capping the amount individuals can give to political parties, and there is a bill going through parliament on elections law that could be used to legislate for this. But the main unions were not in favour, because they worried the law could be extended to outlaw union donations to the Labour party, and over the summer No 10 let it be known Burnham was not in favour of a cap. As Kiran Stacey reported in his story at the time:
double quotation markThose close to the process say capping donations is not a priority for Burnham and not a subject over which it would be worth triggering a fight with Labour’s biggest backers.
At that point, the idea that Reform UK might get donations worth almost as much as $100m probably seemed a bit fanciful.
Not any longer.

The news that Reform UK has received £72m from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires, could have a transformative effect on British politics. It has certainly revived the debate about whether the government should legislate for a cap. Today union leaders are all at the TUC conference in Brighton, and peers are debating the representation of the people bill.

Reform UK insists it will be able to keep the money. “These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it’s going to be in the future,” Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson said yesterday.

But ministers are hinting that the party could be forced to pay the money back. In March this year (when Delo and Harborne were assumed to be living abroad) the government announced that Britons living abroad would only be able to donate £100,000 a year and that, although the law had yet to be passed, it would be apply retrospectively from the date of the announcement, 25 March.

What if donors scuttled back quickly? In July the government announced that there would be “a new timebound cap on large political donations from people who have recently moved to the UK, in effect creating a minimum amount of time someone must permanently be based in the country before they can donate over the cap to a political party or candidate”. This means Britons returning from abroad to live in the UK will have to have been here for at least a year before they are exempt from the £100,000 cap and able to donate as much as they want.

In interviews yesterday, Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said these new laws – which are part of the representation of the people bill still going through parliament – would apply retrospectively. But she would not say directly whether that meant they would apply to the Delo and Harborne donations, and no one seems to know for sure – because Reform UK has not said exactly when Delo and Harborne relocated to the UK.
This has not stopped Reform UK accusing the government of using “dictatorship” tactics. This is what Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader, told Times Radio this morning.

double quotation markWe’re completely confident that [the Delo and Harborne] donations comply with not only the existing rules, but they also comply with the rules currently going through parliament, albeit with that retrospective element … Unless [Labour] literally try and change the rules again as it’s going through the House of Lords, in which case it would have to go back to the Commons. I mean, anything’s possible with this sort of dictatorship currently ruining the country. You know, we’re the victims of a coup.
Tice also accused the Labour of “hypocrisy”. He told ITV’s Good Morning Britain:

double quotation markThese donations are made in accordance with the rules and the regulations, and you’ve now got a hyperventilating hypocrisy from the socialists ruining this country, who are trying to change the rules retrospectively, which is it’s not the fair way, it’s not the British way, and I think most people will say ‘does that just mean that Labour are terrified of the progress of Reform and they’re trying to create an unlevel playing field?’

Given that it is thought Delo and Harborne were living abroad until fairly recently, it does look as though a retrospective law saying that it would be illegal for anyone to give more than £100,000 to a political party now if they have not been living in the UK for at least a year would mean the party would have to hand the money back.

But Reform UK may be gambing on the fact that a legal battle over this could take years. (Historically, the courts have taken a dim view of legislation that looks as if it penalises individuals.) In any legal battle, Reform UK could now easily outspend the Electoral Commission on KCs. And, if they were to win the next election, this would all become irrelevant anyway. There is no mechanism for re-running a general election if it later transpires it was won by a party breaking funding rules.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: The second day of the TUC conference starts in Brighton. Paul Nowak, the general secretary, is speaking at about 11am, and Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, speaks at about 3pm.

11am: John Swinney, the SNP Scottish first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Plaid Cymru Welsh first minister, and Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin Northern Ireland first minister, hold a joint press conference in Cardiff where they are demanding their parliaments and assemblies have the right to hold referendums on leaving the UK.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 3pm: Peers debate the second reading of the representation of the people bill.
Afternoon: Andy Burnham is holding a roundtable meeting with business leaders in Downing Street, ahead of holding a larger reception for CEOs.
