articles.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?
articles.summary: Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime…

image.caption: Iran is looking beyond its southern ports as it seeks alternative routes for trade and importsImage: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Can land corridors offset the impact of the maritime blockade on Iran? The US-led maritime blockade targeting Iranian ports has severely disrupted trade through its southern ports, but it is also accelerating a strategy Tehran had discussed for years: moving more commerce through northern ports, railways and land corridors.

Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh, visiting Moscow for talks with Russian officials, said Iran should activate its northern borders and shift a significant share of imports and exports away from the country's southern maritime routes.

The idea is straightforward. Iran has seven land neighbors, access to the Caspian Sea and several routes linking it to Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and the Caucasus. In theory, that gives Tehran more options than a country dependent on a single maritime gateway.
The question is whether those routes have enough capacity to replace what is being lost at sea.

blocks.caption: Iran's southern ports, like the Port of Bandar Abbas shown here, have traditionally handled the bulk of the country's maritime tradeImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Northern routes offer room to expand
Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, told DW that Iran does have unused capacity.
"Iran has more room to maneuver than its dependence on southern ports might suggest,” he said.

Iranian authorities said in late 2025 that the country's northern ports had more than 30 million tons of nominal annual capacity, with less than one-third in use. That suggests room for more grain, food and general cargo through the Caspian Sea.
Turkey provides another route toward Europe. Rail freight between Iran and Turkey depends partly on train ferries across Lake Van, which carried about 477,000 tons in 2024.

To the northeast, Sarakhs and Incheh Borun connect Iran through Turkmenistan toward Central Asia, Russia and potentially China. To the northwest, Astara is part of the International North-South Transport Corridor linking Iran to Azerbaijan and Russia, he said.

The Astara freight terminal is designed for 3.5 to 4 million tons a year, but handled only about 345,000 tons in the first five months of 2026. The unfinished Rasht-Astara rail link remains an important bottleneck.
For specific goods, these routes matter. Grain from Russia and Kazakhstan, medicines, industrial inputs and regional trade can be redirected more easily than crude oil.

blocks.caption: Freight trains are a key part of Iran's efforts to expand trade through overland routes Image: Amir/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volume is the main obstacle

Jafar Ghaderi, a member of Iranian parliament's Economic Commission, recently said that 83% of what he described as Iran's 210 million tons of imports had traditionally moved through southern maritime borders, a tremendous volume of goods.
"Whenever we are under a maritime blockade, we face problems," hhe said. "How much capacity do our eastern, western and northern corridors actually have?"

The cost difference is also large. Majidreza Hariri, head of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce, said shipping one container from China to Iran through southern ports costs about $3,000 (€2,580), and that moving the same container overland costs roughly $12,000.
With around 2 million containers entering through the south annually, Hariri estimated that a prolonged shift to land routes could add about $18 billion to Iran's trading costs.
Salavati said the physical arithmetic helps explain why.

A 50,000-ton shipload would require around 2,000 truck journeys if each lorry carried 25 tons. Those trucks would then be unavailable for domestic distribution, while longer journeys increase fuel, insurance, warehousing and border costs.
Low-value goods are particularly vulnerable because transport expenses account for a larger share of their final price.

blocks.caption: Maritime cargo volumes are difficult to replicate via rail and road corridorsImage: Rouzbeh Fouladi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Energy is much harder to reroute
Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said Iranian officials are often discussing two different kinds of alternatives.
One involves alternative navigation lanes around Hormuz. The other involves shifting trade toward Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, the Caspian region, Jask and Chabahar.
Neither provides a full substitute for southern energy exports.
A large crude tanker can carry roughly 1.5 to 2 million barrels. Replicating that volume by road would require thousands of tanker trucks.
Rail is more efficient, but still cannot match the cost, speed or scale of maritime transport.
Pakistan can help move imports through Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Iraq can support regional trade and limited fuel flows. Caspian routes can connect Iran to Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.
But none can replace large-scale crude shipments to Asian buyers.
"So the plan is realistic as a resilience strategy, but not as a replacement strategy,” Shokri told DW.
How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz?
Jask pipeline shows both potential and limits
The Goreh-Jask pipeline was built specifically to reduce Iran's dependence on the Strait of Hormuz by moving crude to the Gulf of Oman.
That gives Jask greater strategic importance than most overland corridors.
But Shokri says actual usable capacity has remained far below the project's original ambition.
The lesson is broader: building a pipeline is not the same as creating a functioning export system. Storage, terminals, buyers, insurance, security and financial settlement all have to work together.
Fixed infrastructure also creates new vulnerabilities during wartime.

blocks.caption: Energy infrastructure can improve resilience, but fixed assets such as pipelines also create new vulnerabilities during conflictImage: Ahmad Halabisaz/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: A resilience strategy, not an escape route
Land corridors can help Iran keep essential economic activity alive.
They can move food, medicine, industrial inputs and some regional exports. They can also deepen Iran's economic links with Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq.
If investment continues, the blockade may accelerate infrastructure projects that Tehran had previously treated as long-term opportunities.
But these routes come with higher costs, limited capacity and their own political dependencies.
For Iran, that means the blockade could leave a lasting structural effect by pushing trade away from the south and making northern and overland connections more important.
It does not mean Iran can replace maritime trade.

The corridors can reduce vulnerability, distribute risk and buy time. They cannot reproduce the scale of the Persian Gulf ports and seaborne energy exports on which much of Iran's economy has long depended.

articles.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
articles.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet,…

image.caption: One quarter of Berlin's residents do not have German citizenship and therefore no right to voteImage: Winfried Rothermel/IMAGO

blocks.text: Abdu Taviq, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Taviq is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly annoying at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.
"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to kindergartens and German courses, for example, affect me directly."
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet
Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.
Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's upcoming election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, this will be a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

blocks.caption: Around a third of adults in Stefanie Remlinger's district don't have German nationality Image: Annette Hauschild

blocks.text: Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Taviq is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.
How Berliners are reshaping their city for the future
Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Taviq decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership says it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.
Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.

Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens. (Though that happens to be another one of Taviq's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response.")

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.
More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Taviq, but, in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: AI-linked stocks fall after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development
articles.summary: Shares in tech firms tumble across Asia with Nasdaq also likely to dip later after Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX leaders back call

blocks.text: AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.

Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer of OpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chip makers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.

In Taipei, shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%. Futures for the Nasdaq pointed to a 1.3% drop in the tech-heavy index when the US stock market opens this afternoon.
The sell-off comes after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”.
He said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.

Amodei’s claims have been disputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.
The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support for Amodei’s essay on slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.
Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.

Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world has laws sufficient to contain them.

However, Donald Trump rejected the calls to pace AI development. The US president told reporters over the weekend: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.

“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.”
after newsletter promotion

“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.

“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”
Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.

The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year.
OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 due to safety concerns with the technology.

articles.title: Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank
articles.summary:
Report by Israeli human rights group says systematic and broad assault being waged on conditions required for Palestinians’ existence

Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination”…
articles.byline: Quique Kierszenbaum in Sair, and Peter Beaumont

blocks.text: Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination” of the conditions that sustain Palestinian collective life in the occupied West Bank, according to a major report published by the human rights group B’Tselem.

The Israeli organisation’s hard-hitting report, shared with the Guardian in advance of publication, says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank”, including “the ability to get to work, take children to school or university, receive medical treatment or municipal services, meet family and friends, cultivate land or go on vacation … routine activities that make up human life”.

According to B’Tselem, the assault on Palestinians is “governed by a coherent organising logic” and comprises five “interwoven domains of action”: violence and intimidation, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.

The publication of the Elimination Project, B’Tselem’s most comprehensive piece of work on the West Bank since its launch in 1989, comes less than a week after the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, accused settler terrorists, supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, of committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, in the UK’s starkest condemnation of Israel since the foundation of the state.
1,107Number of Palestinians killed by Israel in the West Bank since October 2023

By looking more broadly at the conditions required for Palestinians’ collective existence, however, the B’Tselem report goes further still. It says various arms of the Israeli state – led by Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister with broad powers over civilian matters in the West Bank – are seeking to “create a reality in which millions of Palestinians live in constant fear of Israeli military and civilian violence”.

“Palestinian communities are being pushed out in an accelerating process of ethnic cleansing, while an ever-expanding Israeli presence is being established in their place in the form of settlements, outposts, farms and Jewish-only civilian infrastructure,” the report says. “Elimination in this context means sustained harm to the conditions that enable Palestinians to exist as a people with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history, and a social and political horizon.

“It is an ongoing political project that seeks to re-organise space and the conditions of life so that Jewish presence becomes contiguous, institutionalised and permanent, while Palestinian existence becomes fragmented, vulnerable and dependent.”
One of the most obvious aspects of this fragmentation is the closure of roads and villages to Palestinian passage, and the abandonment of Palestinian homes under relentless pressure.

On a recent afternoon outside the village of Sair, Haytham Adnan Murad, 49, was returning from a hospital appointment in Hebron with his 12-year-old daughter, Balqis, who is unable to walk because of recent surgery. A gate to the road accessing his village, open in the morning, had been closed by the Israeli army, forcing Murad to get out of the taxi he was travelling in with his daughter and carry her around the roadblock.

blocks.caption: Haytham Adnan Murad carrying his daughter, Balqis, around an Israeli roadblock. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “When we left, the gate was open. Now it’s closed, but this is daily life,” he said. “In the morning, things are different from the afternoon. There’s no dignity in this.”

The authors of the report link the acceleration of the Israeli assault on life in the West Bank to the period after the Hamas attack on southern Israeli communities on 7 October 2023. However, they argue that the underlying motivating ideology predates this period.

In particular they point to a document known as the Decisive Plan, published by Smotrich in 2017, before he became a minister, which they describe as the “key document for understanding Israeli action in the West Bank.”
64 Number of entire communities forcibly displaced in the West Bank since October 2023

B’Tselem says the plan gave Palestinians three options: “Live under Jewish supremacy while relinquishing their national claims, leave the territory, or face violent suppression by the Israeli military if they resist”. It has been translated, the report adds, “into policy, budgets, powers and practices exercised by different arms of the state” with “unprecedented speed and openness”.
As such, the report goes on, settler violence is no longer “operating only as private violence or a breach of public order” but as part of a “broader system of control”.
“It is sometimes carried out alongside soldiers, with the backing of security forces, using weapons, equipment and infrastructure supplied by the state, and with almost complete impunity.”

Beyond the already well-documented incidents of escalating settler violence, the report highlights other corrosive aspects of the tightening Israeli grip on the West Bank, including devastating economic restrictions, and impacts on education and culture.
31.3%Unemployment rate in the West Bank in 2024, up from 13.1% in 2022

Israel, it says, has enacted a systematic policy of “full economic strangulation” since 2023, which has denied livelihood opportunities, destroyed civilian and agricultural infrastructure, tightened control over resources and the banking system, and undermined the ability of public institutions to provide basic services.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian shepherd from the hamlet of Anizan, where residents have been repeatedly driven out of their homes by settlers. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Smotrich said in September 2025 he would employ every means possible “to prevent the danger of a Palestinian state, including bringing about the collapse of the Palestinian Authority … through economic strangulation”.

Mass work permit revocations have left workers and their families without a stable income. This is reflected in data from the West Bank cited in the report. The unemployment rate, for instance, rose from 13.1% in 2022 to 31.3% in 2024, and in 2025, nearly half of all young people were neither employed nor enrolled in education or vocational training.
The UN has estimated that in 2024, 700,000 Palestinians in the West Bank needed assistance to buy food, a 17% increase from the previous year.

Since October 2023, Israel has also intensified attacks on various Palestinian organisations and associations in the West Bank. Grassroots and community groups, as well as organisations that protect workers, people in need and children, have faced frequent raids on their offices, forced closure, systematic harassment and the arrest of employees, volunteers and activists without cause.
Cogat, the Israeli military unit responsible for overseeing civilian policy in the West Bank and Gaza, has been approached for comment.
8 to 20%Proportion of West Bank schools closed in the 2023-24 academic year

In an interview conducted to coincide with the report’s publication, Kareem Jubran, the head of B’Tselem’s field research on the West Bank, said: “What we uncovered is that these are not separate incidents. All the disparate elements have one character, one goal. When you look at the picture from above, it leads to one conclusion: that the main goal is to eliminate Palestinians as a collective.”

blocks.caption: The remnants of the Palestinian shepherds’ village of al-Qabun after settler violence forced its inhabitants to leave. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Yuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem, said: “What we are saying in the report is that this is ongoing. The project was there before, but now we are in a new phase.

“It started at the end of 2022, with the change of the government [to a right-far right coalition], and we saw another marked escalation after October 2023. What we are talking about is an attack on Palestinian life in the West Bank that changed in scale. It’s as much a quantitative element that has changed, making the West Bank more and more unlivable for many Palestinians.”

Novak described Smotrich’s plan from 2017 as the “blueprint”. “It shows the ideological and the operational way to get to what we are calling an elimination,” he said. “And he calls it victory by settlement. To win in a very final way so that nothing [such as a Palestinian state] can happen afterwards.”
All data and figures provided by B’Tselem

articles.title: Bali police investigate after Australian man and children found dead in home
articles.summary: Police were called after the man's wife became concerned and asked neighbours to check on her family.

blocks.text: Police in Bali are investigating after the bodies of an Australian man and his two children were found dead in their bungalow in a popular tourist area.
Damien John Shaw, 56, and his two children, a boy aged six and a girl aged four, were found dead in their home in Kuta on Sunday.
Police said neighbours had checked in on the family after a call from the man's wife, who had become concerned after a phone call with her husband. She was not in Bali at the time.

Australian media reported that police were treating the case as a suspected murder-suicide. Police told the BBC they had not yet determined the cause or manner of death and that further examinations would be carried out.
Police said the man's wife had called a neighbour after hearing one of her children crying while on the phone to her husband. She was subsequently unable to contact him again.
His wife had reportedly travelled to the capital Jakarta in the previous days.

Police said that the neighbour, accompanied by other local residents, had then forced their way into the property after there was no response to their knocks. The three victims were discovered inside.
Police said Shaw was originally from Fremantle in Western Australia. Roger Cook, the state's premier, described the news as a "very confronting situation".
"This is a very sad situation; our hearts go out to everyone involved. We hope we can get to the bottom of what's gone on as soon as possible," he added.

articles.title: Canada seeks 'unique alliance' with EU, Carney says
articles.summary: Mark Carney clarified Canada's EU ambitions amid a WSJ report that Ottawa was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc.

image.caption: Canada has already increased its closeness with the EUImage: Andrej Ivanov/AFP

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday said he was pursuing unprecedented closeness with the European Union to reduce its dependence on its economically hostile neighbor, but not a membership with the bloc.
"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival.

"What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — is a unique ​alliance between Canada and the European Union," he said. "We share the same values, we have the same priorities and ​we have very complementary strengths."

Carney's clarification came after a report by the Wall Street Journal claimed he was exploring whether Canada could become an "associate member" of the bloc. The newspaper reported that the EU was open to the idea of granting Canada associate membership — a status it would have to create for the North American nation.
Zelenskyy strengthens defense ties with Canada
Carney's mission EU
The remarks precede the Canadian prime minister's scheduled trip to France this week.
In Strasbourg, France, Carney will become the first head of government to attend the "State of the European Union" address before delivering his own speech at the European Parliament.
His visit is a "tremendous symbol," said Tobias Cremer, a European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a March resolution calling for stronger EU-Canada cooperation.
"Canada has many of the resources that Europe is very much short of, whether it's in terms of energy, whether it's rare earths (and) raw minerals," Cremer said.
Canada is already the first non-EU Nation to join the bloc's defense procurement program, while Carney was involved in Canada joining the Eurovision Song Contest for 2027.
Meanwhile, Montreal is set to host an EU-Canada summit where Carney said discussions will begin on building a "much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership."
Canada's increasing closeness with the EU comes when the country is in the middle of an escalating trade war with its largest trading partner and neighbor, the United States.

articles.title: Germany: Merz's CDU comes out on top in Lower Saxony polls
articles.summary: The Christian Democrats have emerged as the strongest party at local elections in the state of Lower Saxony. The vote was closely watched as an indicator of the strength of the far-right AfD, which…

image.caption: Chancellor Merz's CDU has won local elections in Lower SaxonyImage: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has remained the strongest force at district level in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony following local elections there, preliminary results released on Monday show.

The elections on Sunday received an unusual degree of attention, as they were seen as a gauge of support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) following its landslide win in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last week.
The elections were to choose mayors, district administrations and local councils in the state.
What were the election results in Lower Saxony?

In what will doubtless be a relief for under-pressure Chancellor Friedrich Merz, his CDU came in first with 27.2% of the vote, slightly down on the 31.7% it reached in the last local elections in Lower Saxony in 2021.
The Social Democrats (SPD), who lead a coalition government at state level, were in second place with 24.6% support, a sharp drop from the 30% achieved in 2021.
The AfD followed with 15.9%, more than tripling its result in 2021.
The Greens, who are the junior coalition partners at state level, were on 14.1%, compared with 15.9% in 2021.
The Left party and the Free Democrats (FDP) brought up the tail with 6% and 3.7% respectively.
High turnout in Lower Saxony
Some 6.3 million people were eligible to take part in the elections, which saw a turnout of 64.6%, well up on the 57% participation at the 2021 polls.
Any run-off elections will take place across the state on September 27.

The poll in Lower Saxony was seen not only as a test of public sentiment ahead of state elections next year but also as a barometer of how the AfD is currently faring in western German states, where the far-right party has less support than in the east.
The elections in the state come just a week before the next state polls in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and the city-state of Berlin.
The vote in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will be under especially close scrutiny, with the AfD expected to make strong gains while the CDU is polling at just 7%.

articles.title: Hyrox athlete sparks debate for continuing race after soiling herself
articles.summary: Some have raised concerns around hygiene while others saluted her resolve to finish the race.

blocks.text: An athlete's Hyrox performance has sparked debate after completing a race in Beijing despite soiling herself midway through the event.

Footage of the woman competing in the indoor fitness competition despite her soiled legs has gone viral, with some people raising concerns around hygiene and others saluting her resolve to push through. Some also criticised race organisers for letting her to continue.
Hyrox said they launched a "major cleanup operation" after the event on Saturday, including by sanitising equipment and replacing sections of the carpet.
The German fitness company acknowledged the "legitimate concerns" but urged people not to direct their frustration at the athlete herself.
The company did not reveal the woman's identity, but it was revealed online and she subsequently received threats of violence.
"There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete," Hyrox said in a statement early on Monday.
"Any person identified as engaging in this behaviour – whether through comments, direct messages or social media – will be permanently banned from all Hyrox events," it said.
Some participants in the same event had demanded an apology and a refund, arguing that they were forced to come into contact with contaminated equipment, Chinese media reported.
In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, such as the sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world.
Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including spitting and littering.

"From a basic health and sanitation standpoint, the athlete should have been stopped immediately, and any contaminated areas should have been closed off and properly cleaned before other athletes were allowed through," Erica Dodge, a US-based nurse, wrote in a comment on Instagram.

Joe Ho, who also took part in the Hyrox Beijing competition over the weekend, has criticised Hyrox's response to the issue and called on the organisation to "take responsibility when its own procedures fail".
"If the organisation accepts that something went wrong, why not offer affected participants refunds, credits, or some meaningful form of compensation?" he wrote.
Others in the fitness community have pointed out that this is not unheard of for endurance athletes.
One comment on Facebook, whose author noted that marathoners have similar experiences, while another wrote: "They've trained too long and too hard to give up just like that."

In 2005, British marathoner Paula Radcliffe famously stopped at the 22-mile mark during the London Marathon to relieve herself by the side of the road in full view of cameras and then went on to win the race.
Earlier this year, Chinese marathoner Li Meizhen made headlines after crossing the finish line at the Hengshui Lake Marathon with menstrual blood on her legs.

articles.title: Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA
articles.summary: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’

blocks.text: Israel’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of NAZA, a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.

In the film, the Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza that have killed tens of thousands of civilians. In one interview, a source claims that approval had been given to kill 500 NAZA in order to kill one Hamas member.
The 80-minute documentary won a special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record.
On Sunday Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors on X of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.
“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.
Other Israeli ministers also took aim at the directors, who won an Oscar in 2025 for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
“You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said on X.
“I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms.”

The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, although it is rarely applied. In 2022 the supreme court confirmed that the state may strip people of their nationality if they have failed to show “loyalty”, for example by committing acts of espionage or treason.
The law was also expanded in 2023 to apply to people convicted of “terrorism”.
The law requires the interior minister to submit the revocation request, the justice minister to approve it and judges to validate it.
Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob after the world premiere of 2024’s No Other Land, which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank.

“We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic,” he told the Guardian, adding: “For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons.
“Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”

The Israeli military has responded to NAZA by saying it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary and criticised the use of anonymous testimonies, saying the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified”.

The Palestinian militant group Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Hamas militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza.
The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the subsequent three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties.
– Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: The Debut is going to win an Oscar
articles.summary: The Debut is a movie that blends comedy, horror and drama so effectively it’s impossible to define it as one. And it's a movie that does so by showcasing one of the most incredible, and endearing,…

image.caption: Julianne Moore appears as Mona in The Debut. (NOC Productions Inc. LLC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

The Debut is a movie that blends comedy, horror and drama so effectively it’s impossible to define it as one. And it's a movie that does so by showcasing one of the most incredible, and endearing, acting tour-de-forces of a lifetime from Julianne Moore.
Jesse Eisenberg directed film starring Julianne Moore is a tour de force

Every year, there are Oscar-bait films: stories designed to play on the emotions and sentimentalities of a voting body that seem to care more about how artistic a movie feels than actually is. And every year, audiences turn against them as contrived, out of touch and desperate.

Which you'd think could bode poorly for Julianne Moore, star of writer-director Jesse Eisenberg's The Debut — at least when it comes to how regular audiences might feel about a performance best described as "psychotically genius."

Because on its face, the chaotic, carnivalesque community theatre parable presents with all the risk factors: entertainment about the world of entertainment, absurdist high-minded comedy that feels straight out of a New Yorker cartoon, and a main character that reads like a cross between Patti LuPone in Evita and Joaquin Phoenix in Joker.

In short, it's the kind of thing that might feel designed in a lab to win an Oscar — and therefore, come off as annoyingly self-important to actual audiences when they get to see it. But on that front, there are two bits of good news for The Debut. The first is that this thing is almost definitely going to nab that Oscar. And the second is that it won’t do it by being disingenuous.

Because this is quite clearly one of the most shatteringly good movies of the year; a film that blends comedy, horror and drama so effectively it’s impossible to define it as any one genre. And it's a movie that does so by showcasing one of the most incredible, and endearing, acting tour-de-forces of a lifetime.

The Debut is anchored by Moore's stunning, unrestrained performance as Mona — despite, initially, seeming as shallow as it gets. A demure housewife with two near-adult children and emotionally immature husband, Mona apparently hasn’t been given the privilege of developing an interior life. Instead, she seems to have spent the past 50 or so years in the painfully simple, almost fableistic role constructed around her.

She makes dinner for an unappreciative family in a house that looks like it was decorated by a cross between Martha Stewart and Doctor Seuss. She goes to weekly cocktail nights with a couple who don't even pretend to hear her speak. And when she talks, she does so in a quiet, plain, sing-song voice that practically screams "please don’t be mad at me." Not that she has the confidence to scream about anything, to anyone at all.

That is, until she decides to audition for a community theatre production of Nosy Neighbors — a fictional musical about all the zany inhabitants of a seedy apartment building, in which she would play building super Ms. Danielle.

It's an obviously good-spirited takedown of plays in the style of 7 Stories and The Dining Room —the ensemble-based, zany-characters-share-a-single-location-type of stories that tend to clog up community theatre calendars. It's a refreshing specificity only someone familiar with community theatre would know: the perennial struggle to find plays with enough jokes to go around for everyone auditioning.

That is Eisenberg to a tee. Having done community theatre from six years old, he's spoken about his love for the types of people you encounter there often, and worked on it, too: his 2019 off-Broadway play Happy Talk cast Susan Sarandon as a musical-worshipping suburban housewife, slavishly obsessed with her role in a rinky-dink staging of South Pacific. Like Mona, she is a woman who talks incessantly about her star turn as if she's Liza Minnelli in Cabaret, though to a husband — and by extension, world — that refuses to notice.

The self-evidently pathetic tragedy of a woman scrambling for meaning and recognition universally denied her is the exact same theme returned to in The Debut. Because as Mona blithers on about her own upcoming role, there’s only one problem: she’s terrible. Comically terrible. Cosmically, incomparably bad in a way that increasingly suggests there's something deeper, more disturbing wrong with her.

items: Apple TV's Mayday is propaganda — and it rocks
Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars bombs at the box office. Here's what that tells us about what audiences want

blocks.text: It's a problem that at first, washed-up, big-fish-little-pond director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) feels he can coach out of her. The bizarre trajectory that follows is better seen than read about, though it's an obvious homage to films centred on delusional, self-obsessed characters like The King of Comedy, Taxi Driver and, yes, Joker give Moore an infinitely fertile playground to do things most actors only dream of.

And it is all done as her character seeks to find truth in fiction at literally any cost, like a more-than-half-crazed Uta Hagen — the iconic teacher who influenced a generation of actors to invent and know nearly every aspect of their entire character's life. Even if they only delivered one line.

It is an approach Mona, who starts with no life of her own, takes to the most terrifying conclusion. The kaleidoscopic, astonishing, horribly hilarious journey it takes her on is not quite of the laugh-until-you-cry variety; it's maybe closer to cry-until-you-laugh. Or maybe do both simultaneously until you forget what you were feeling in the first place.
Absent inner life

Here, Moore portrays a woman whose inner life and self-worth was so completely strangled they appeared to have atrophied into nothing. And then that burst forward with such propellant, stunning force you are nearly blinded by looking at the screen.

It’s largely accomplished by Eisenberg's tightly efficient, but confidently assured writing, which is both effectively engineered and feels so loose it seems nearly like improvisation; we are given just enough hints at Mona’s backstory without being spoonfed, and allowed to draw our own ludicrous conclusions.

The supporting cast is also uniquely excellent; alongside the heartbreakingly effective two-hander between Giamatti (channelling the tough-mentor success of The Holdovers) and Moore, the Nosy Neighbors cast and crew more than hold her own. Halle Bailey's casting as the play's lead lets her showcase her pipes and acting palette. While up-and-comer Eldar Isgandarov, playing easily-cowed assistant Piotr, flexes the comedic muscles he also shows off in the equally incredible Club Kid, which is also playing at TIFF.
Film industry has built 'solid bridge' between Canada and U.S., says TIFF CEO
But again, this is Moore’s show — one where she expands the cliche, male-dominated archetype of unhinged, at-the-fringes desperado with aplomb.

The result is an acting performance for the ages. A chameleonic cycle of transformations that should, and will, go down in the history books. And one that situates her in a uniquely comfortable position when it comes to the Oscars race. Because Moore in The Debut is something to behold, and seems impossible to ignore.
And most importantly, it all seems genuine.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Germany's Zverev wins US Open in golden year
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev has won the US Open for the first time, defeating Ben Shelton in the final. It is Zverev's second Grand Slam win of 2026 after a long wait for his first title, but controversy still…

image.caption: After waiting for years to win his first major title, Zverev has now won 2 this yearImage: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: Alexander Zverev has won his second Grand Slam singles title after the German top seed beat Ben Shelton in the final of the US Open on Sunday.
Zverev beat the American, who was making his first appearance in a major final, 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2.

This success caps the best season of Zverev's career. Not only has he now won two of the four Grand Slams in the same season, but he has become just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

"We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now we've won two in three months," Zverev said on court after his second major win of the year, following his victory at the French Open in June.
"God has seen how hard we've worked and how much we've suffered. 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before," he said as he thanked his coaching team and family.
Great expectations from the start

As a former junior world No. 1, there were great expectations on Zverev from the moment he started his pro career in 2013 at just 16 years old. Titles soon followed, as did a shock early win over Roger Federer in a tournament in his native Germany in 2016.

blocks.caption: Zverev is starting to deliver on the promise he has shown throughout his careerImage: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: But the presence of Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic meant Zverev struggled to make a mark in the Grand Slams. After a string of disappointing exits, he had something of a breakthrough in 2020, reaching the semifinals of the Australian Open and the final of the US Open.

With age starting to catch up with at least two of the big three in modern men's tennis, Zverev looked well primed to become a dominant force in the majors. His 2021 Olympic gold felt like it might be just the start.
French Open ends long grand slam wait

But he was unable to make the opportunity count, and the emergence of Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has made the task even tougher. Finally, this year, Zverev got his hands on a major title, winning at Roland Garros in June. In doing so, he became the first German man to win a singles Grand Slam since Boris Becker in 1996 in the process.

"It was just relief, joy, everything together," he told ATPTour.com. "I didn't realize that I had won the match until I saw my box all jumping around and celebrating. In your mind, you think, 'Well I've got to continue playing', but then I saw my dad raise his arms in the air. That's when it kind of hit me, 'Okay, we've done it. We've achieved it. We are Grand Slam champions'."

Becker's triumph was a year before Zverev was born in Hamburg to Russian parents who were both tennis pros in the Soviet Union and moved to Germany in 1991. His older brother, Mischa, was also a pro until 2023, reaching the quarterfinals of the Australian Open in 2017 and becoming world number 25 in the same year. But it was Alexander who was destined for the even bigger stage.
Family a big influence on Zverev's career

In their youth, Mischa was generally coached by his father, Alexander Zverev Snr, while the younger brother was coached by his mother, Irina. His father has taken the reins in the professional arena though, and the family remain a constant fixture at Zverev's matches.

"I know there are crazy tennis parents out there as well," the 29-year-old said on the subject ahead of the US Open. "If you try to control every single aspect of your kid's life, even when the kid is 25, 26, 27 years old and at some point has a personal life… I think that is never helpful."

"But if you have smart tennis parents like we do have on tour now, I feel like Ben Shelton's father is incredibly smart, Casper Ruud's father is incredibly smart, I feel like I'm lucky enough to say the same thing about my parents. I think then it's beneficial."

blocks.caption: Zverev's triumph in the French Open this year was his first grand slam winImage: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite finally ending Germany's long wait for a major male tennis champion, Zverev is far from universally liked in his own country, or on the tennis circuit.
Domestic violence allegations

While there is acknowledgement of his work in promoting awareness of type 1 diabetes, with which he was diagnosed in 2022, allegations of domestic abuse have hung over his career and seen him heckled at various tournaments. His behavior on court has also seen him get in trouble before.

The first came in October 2020, when his ex-girlfriend, Olya Sharypova, claimed he had been violent towards her on multiple occasions. However, Sharypova didn't press criminal charges, and in January 2023, men's tennis governing body the ATP closed its own investigation into the matter, citing "insufficient evidence."
Welcoming that decision at the time, Zverev said: "From the beginning, I have maintained my innocence and denied the baseless allegations made against me."

But he faced a Berlin court in 2024 after similar allegations from Brenda Patea, Zverev's ex-girlfriend and the mother of his daughter. The court was told that "after a heated argument" in the German capital, Zverev allegedly pushed Patea against a wall and strangled her with both hands.

He denied the charges and the case was settled, with Zverev paying €200,000 ($233,000), €150,000 of which went to the state and €50,000 to charitable organizations. The case was officially declared "no verdict" and Zverev made no admission of guilt.
